subject: ss-critical-care
title: Modes of mechanical ventilation and waveforms

steps.tx: **Volume control** sets tidal volume and flow, and airway pressure varies with compliance and resistance. **Pressure control** sets inspiratory pressure and time, and tidal volume falls when the lung stiffens. The clinician has to notice a falling volume on a pressure breath, because the ventilator will not alarm on volume unless a limit was set.
steps.say: Volume control sets tidal volume and flow, and airway pressure varies with compliance and resistance. Pressure control sets inspiratory pressure and time, and tidal volume falls when the lung stiffens. The clinician has to notice a falling volume on a pressure breath, because the ventilator will not alarm on volume unless a limit was set.

steps.tx: **Pressure support** is a spontaneous mode. The patient triggers every breath, and the breath cycles when inspiratory flow falls to a set fraction of peak flow. There is no guaranteed rate unless backup apnoea ventilation is on. A patient who is tiring can look comfortable for a few minutes and then stop triggering.

vis.alt: Pressure, flow, and volume sketches for assist control, SIMV with a spontaneous breath, and pressure support.
vis.caption: Assist control shows a patient trigger on a delivered breath. SIMV shows mandatory breaths with one spontaneous breath between them. Pressure support shows flow-cycled breaths and no set rate. Volume control versus pressure control is not labelled as such. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.tx: **SIMV** is a mix of mandatory breaths and spontaneous breaths. It is not a weaning mode. The added work of breathing on the spontaneous breaths delays liberation, because those breaths are often poorly supported. A falling mandatory rate is not the same as a spontaneous breathing trial. Readiness is tested by a trial, not by stretching SIMV over days.

steps.tx: **PRVC**, or pressure regulated volume control, targets a tidal volume by adjusting inspiratory pressure from breath to breath. It is still a pressure breath, and a sudden cough can make the ventilator drop the pressure and underdeliver. The set volume is a target, not a guarantee, on the breath the patient is fighting.

steps.tx: **APRV** uses a long high pressure time and a short release. The short release generates auto-PEEP, which is part of how the mode holds the lung open. It is not first line ARDS ventilation. Rescue use is a senior decision after lung protective ventilation has already been done properly, not a starting mode.

vis.caption: These are the phases of diffuse alveolar damage. APRV is not drawn. The histology is not a reason to choose APRV, and the lesson does not use it as first line ventilation. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.tx: **NAVA** is scaled in proportion to the diaphragmatic electrical signal. **Proportional assist** ventilation assists in proportion to measured effort. Both need a reliable signal and an awake drive. A poor catheter signal or a patient with no drive makes the mode look like failure of the lung when the problem is the signal.

steps.tx: **Double triggering** stacks two breaths and raises tidal volume. **Reverse triggering** is diaphragmatic effort provoked by the ventilator breath, often under deep sedation, and it also stacks volume. Both can deliver a tidal volume far above the set one. The waveform shows two efforts or two deliveries where one breath was intended.

steps.tx: On a volume breath the flow waveform is set by the clinician, often a **square wave**. On a pressure breath the flow waveform is **decelerating**. Reading the wrong waveform leads to the wrong diagnosis of dyssynchrony. Name the mode before you name the problem, or a normal decelerating flow will be called obstruction.
steps.say: On a volume breath the flow waveform is set by the clinician, often a square wave. On a pressure breath the flow waveform is decelerating. Reading the wrong waveform leads to the wrong diagnosis of dyssynchrony. Name the mode before you name the problem, or a normal decelerating flow will be called obstruction.
